title: EMSCodeSim EMT Flashcard Trainer
description: Free foundational flashcards for future EMT students and EMT learners.
disclaimer: Educational review only. Medication scope, terminology, radio codes, equipment use, and protocols vary by state and agency. Follow your approved EMT course, instructor, medical director, and current local protocols.

cards.back: The study of body structures and how those structures are organized.
cards.note: Example: knowing where the lungs, heart, and major bones are located.

cards.back: The study of how body structures function.
cards.note: Example: understanding how the lungs exchange gases or how the heart moves blood.

cards.back: The smallest living unit of the body. Cells need oxygen and nutrients and must remove waste.
cards.note: Illness or poor perfusion can disrupt normal cell function.

cards.back: A group of similar cells working together for a common purpose.
cards.note: Muscle, nervous, epithelial, and connective tissue are major tissue types.

cards.back: A body structure made of multiple tissue types that performs a specific function.
cards.note: The heart, lungs, brain, liver, and kidneys are organs.

cards.back: A group of organs that work together to perform major body functions.
cards.note: EMS assessment often asks which system may be failing and how that affects the whole patient.

cards.back: The body’s effort to maintain a stable internal environment.
cards.note: Temperature, blood glucose, pH, and blood pressure are examples of values the body regulates.

cards.back: The nose, mouth, jaw, pharynx, and related structures that conduct air toward the lower airway.
cards.note: Swelling, secretions, trauma, or loss of muscle tone can threaten patency.

cards.back: The larynx, trachea, bronchi, bronchioles, and lungs below the upper airway.
cards.note: Wheezing, crackles, and diminished sounds can suggest lower-airway or lung problems.

cards.back: Microscopic air sacs where oxygen and carbon dioxide move between air and blood.
cards.note: Fluid, collapse, or poor ventilation can reduce gas exchange.

cards.back: The major muscle of breathing located beneath the lungs.
cards.note: When it contracts, the chest cavity expands and air is drawn in.

cards.back: The physical movement of air into and out of the lungs.
cards.note: A patient can have oxygen present but still ventilate poorly.

cards.back: Gas exchange: oxygen enters the blood and tissues while carbon dioxide leaves them.
cards.note: External respiration occurs in the lungs; internal respiration occurs at the tissues.

cards.back: The delivery of oxygenated blood to body tissues and organs.
cards.note: Mental status, skin signs, pulse quality, and blood pressure help assess perfusion.

cards.back: Receives deoxygenated blood from the body and pumps it to the lungs.
cards.note: Right-sided failure can contribute to systemic venous congestion.

cards.back: Receives oxygenated blood from the lungs and pumps it to the body.
cards.note: Left-sided failure can contribute to pulmonary congestion and breathing difficulty.

cards.back: A blood vessel that carries blood away from the heart.
cards.note: Most arteries carry oxygenated blood, but the pulmonary arteries carry deoxygenated blood to the lungs.

cards.back: A blood vessel that carries blood toward the heart.
cards.note: Most veins carry deoxygenated blood, but pulmonary veins carry oxygenated blood from the lungs.

cards.back: A tiny vessel where gases, nutrients, and waste products exchange between blood and tissues.
cards.note: Capillary-level perfusion is essential for cell survival.

cards.back: The brain and spinal cord.
cards.note: It processes information and coordinates many body functions.

cards.back: Nerves outside the brain and spinal cord.
cards.note: It carries sensory information to the CNS and motor commands away from it.

cards.back: Bones, joints, muscles, tendons, and ligaments that provide support and movement.
cards.note: Injury can affect movement, circulation, sensation, and the ability to ventilate.

cards.back: The skin, hair, nails, and related structures.
cards.note: Skin color, temperature, moisture, wounds, and burns provide important assessment clues.

cards.back: Organs that break down food, absorb nutrients, and eliminate solid waste.
cards.note: Abdominal pain, vomiting, bleeding, and dehydration can involve this system.

cards.back: The kidneys, ureters, bladder, and urethra; it filters blood and regulates fluid and electrolytes.
cards.note: Reduced urine output can be a clue to poor perfusion or kidney dysfunction.

cards.back: Glands that release hormones to regulate metabolism, growth, stress response, and glucose balance.
cards.note: Diabetes and adrenal emergencies are common EMS-related endocrine concerns.

cards.back: Prefix meaning below, deficient, or less than normal.
cards.note: Examples: hypoglycemia, hypothermia, hypotension.

cards.back: Prefix meaning above, excessive, or more than normal.
cards.note: Examples: hyperglycemia, hyperthermia, hypertension.

cards.back: Prefix meaning slow.
cards.note: Example: bradycardia means a slower-than-expected heart rate.

cards.back: Prefix meaning fast or rapid.
cards.note: Examples: tachycardia and tachypnea.

cards.back: Prefix meaning without or absence of.
cards.note: Examples: apnea means no breathing; anoxia means absence of oxygen.

cards.back: Prefix meaning difficult, painful, or abnormal.
cards.note: Examples: dyspnea and dysrhythmia.

cards.back: Prefix meaning around or surrounding.
cards.note: Example: pericardium is the sac around the heart.

cards.back: Prefix meaning within or inside.
cards.note: Example: endotracheal means within the trachea.

cards.back: Prefix meaning on, upon, or above.
cards.note: Example: epidermis is the outer layer of skin.

cards.back: Prefix meaning within.
cards.note: Examples: intravenous and intraosseous.

cards.back: Prefix meaning below or under.
cards.note: Examples: subcutaneous and sublingual.

cards.back: Prefix meaning many or excessive.
cards.note: Examples: polyuria and polydipsia.

cards.back: Prefix meaning few, scant, or reduced.
cards.note: Example: oliguria means abnormally low urine output.

cards.back: Word root referring to the heart.
cards.note: Examples: cardiology, cardiovascular, cardiogenic.

cards.back: Word roots referring to air, lungs, or breathing.
cards.note: Examples: pneumonia, pneumothorax, pulmonary.

cards.back: Word root referring to nerves or the nervous system.
cards.note: Examples: neurologic and neuropathy.

cards.back: Word roots referring to blood.
cards.note: Examples: hemorrhage, hematoma, hematology.

cards.back: Word root referring to the stomach.
cards.note: Examples: gastritis and gastrointestinal.

cards.back: Word root referring to the liver.
cards.note: Examples: hepatitis and hepatomegaly.

cards.back: Word roots referring to the kidney.
cards.note: Examples: nephrology and renal failure.

cards.back: Word root referring to skin.
cards.note: Examples: dermatitis and dermatology.

cards.back: Word root referring to bone.
cards.note: Examples: osteoporosis and osteomyelitis.

cards.back: Word root referring to muscle.
cards.note: Examples: myocardial and myopathy.

cards.back: Suffix meaning inflammation.
cards.note: Examples: bronchitis, appendicitis, dermatitis.

cards.back: Suffix referring to a condition of the blood.
cards.note: Examples: hypoglycemia and bacteremia.

cards.back: Suffix referring to breathing.
cards.note: Examples: apnea, dyspnea, tachypnea.

cards.back: Suffix meaning pain.
cards.note: Examples: neuralgia and myalgia.

cards.back: Suffix meaning surgical removal.
cards.note: Example: appendectomy.

cards.back: Closer to the trunk or point of attachment.
cards.note: The elbow is proximal to the wrist.

cards.back: Farther from the trunk or point of attachment.
cards.note: The fingers are distal to the elbow.

cards.back: Anterior means toward the front; posterior means toward the back.
cards.note: These terms help describe findings precisely.

cards.back: Medial means toward the midline; lateral means away from the midline.
cards.note: The nose is medial to the eyes.

cards.back: Superior means above; inferior means below.
cards.note: The chest is superior to the abdomen.

cards.back: Basic Life Support: the EMT-level assessment and care system, though exact scope varies by jurisdiction.
cards.note: Use the formal term in documentation rather than assuming everyone uses it identically.

cards.back: Advanced Life Support: care involving advanced assessment, medications, procedures, or paramedic-level resources.
cards.note: What counts as ALS depends on state and local scope.

cards.back: Motor vehicle collision / motor vehicle accident. Many agencies prefer “collision” because it does not assume the event was unavoidable.
cards.note: Use your agency’s approved terminology.

cards.back: Mass-casualty incident: an event where patient needs may exceed immediately available resources.
cards.note: MCI thresholds and triage systems are locally defined.

cards.back: Refusal of medical assistance / against medical advice. Terminology varies.
cards.note: A refusal requires capacity assessment, informed discussion, documentation, and local-protocol compliance.

cards.back: Estimated time of arrival.
cards.note: Give realistic updates and revise them if conditions change.

cards.back: The unit has started traveling toward the assigned location or destination.
cards.note: Radio status wording varies by dispatch system.

cards.back: The unit has arrived at the incident location.
cards.note: Arrival does not automatically mean the scene is safe.

cards.back: Waiting at a designated safe location until the scene is secured or resources are coordinated.
cards.note: Common for violence, hazmat, fire, and large incidents.

cards.back: A local term often meaning lights-and-sirens response.
cards.note: The exact meaning varies; do not assume it is universal.

cards.back: Informal phrase for minimizing scene time when rapid transport is a priority.
cards.note: It does not mean skipping immediate lifesaving care.

cards.back: Informal phrase for performing more treatment before transport.
cards.note: The phrase can oversimplify complex decisions; use clinical priorities and protocol.

cards.back: Informal phrase similar to load and go, often used in time-sensitive trauma.
cards.note: Use professional language around patients and families.

cards.back: A person who accesses EMS repeatedly.
cards.note: Avoid dismissive labels such as “frequent flyer”; repeated calls can reflect unmet medical or social needs.

cards.back: A hospital notification that a patient may need a trauma-team response.
cards.note: Criteria and alert levels vary by system.

cards.back: Informal phrase for active cardiac-arrest resuscitation.
cards.note: Document the actual patient condition and interventions.

cards.back: Return of spontaneous circulation after cardiac arrest.
cards.note: ROSC does not end care; airway, ventilation, perfusion, and transport planning remain priorities.

cards.back: Estimated time from collapse or arrest until resuscitation or circulation.
cards.note: Clarify whether the estimate is witnessed, unwitnessed, no-flow, or total time.

cards.back: Short for mechanism of injury: how traumatic energy was transferred to the patient.
cards.note: Mechanism supports—but does not replace—the physical assessment.

cards.back: The clinician’s level of concern based on history, exam, mechanism, and context.
cards.note: It should be tied to specific findings rather than intuition alone.

cards.back: Hazard-control areas used at incidents such as hazmat or active threats.
cards.note: Definitions and entry requirements are incident-command decisions.

cards.back: Resources requested from another agency or jurisdiction.
cards.note: Use clear resource names and assignments.

cards.back: A meeting between units, often to add an ALS crew or transfer care.
cards.note: Plan a safe location and avoid delays that outweigh the benefit.

cards.back: The unit has completed the call and can accept another assignment.
cards.note: Complete required restocking, cleaning, and documentation according to policy.

cards.back: A hand-operated device used to provide positive-pressure ventilation through a mask or advanced airway.
cards.note: Good technique includes airway positioning, an effective seal, visible chest rise, and avoiding excessive rate or volume.

cards.back: A curved airway adjunct placed in the mouth to help prevent the tongue from obstructing the airway.
cards.note: Generally used in deeply unresponsive patients without an intact gag reflex; follow training and protocol.

cards.back: A soft airway adjunct inserted through a nostril to help maintain an open airway.
cards.note: Contraindications, sizing, lubrication, and insertion technique must follow course instruction and protocol.

cards.back: A device that removes blood, vomit, or secretions from the airway.
cards.note: Check battery, tubing, canister, pressure, and catheter availability during unit checks.

cards.back: A firm, large-bore catheter often used to suction the mouth and oropharynx.
cards.note: It is commonly called a tonsil-tip or Yankauer catheter.

cards.back: A pressurized oxygen source and device that controls flow.
cards.note: Secure cylinders, confirm pressure, inspect the regulator, and keep oil or grease away from oxygen equipment.

cards.back: A low-flow oxygen-delivery device with prongs placed in the nostrils.
cards.note: It is generally better tolerated than a mask, but delivery depends on flow, fit, and patient breathing.

cards.back: An oxygen mask with a reservoir bag and one-way valves designed to deliver a high oxygen concentration to a breathing patient.
cards.note: Inflate the reservoir before application and monitor the bag during inhalation.

cards.back: A device that turns liquid medication into an inhaled mist.
cards.note: Medication, dose, oxygen or air flow, and indications must follow protocol.

cards.back: Continuous positive airway pressure: a noninvasive device that maintains pressure during spontaneous breathing.
cards.note: It can improve oxygenation and reduce work of breathing in selected patients; contraindications matter.

cards.back: A device that estimates peripheral oxygen saturation and pulse rate using light absorption.
cards.note: Treat the patient, not one number; motion, poor perfusion, nail products, and other factors can affect readings.

cards.back: An inflatable cuff used to measure arterial blood pressure.
cards.note: Correct cuff size and placement are essential for useful readings.

cards.back: An acoustic tool used to hear body sounds such as Korotkoff sounds, breath sounds, and some heart sounds.
cards.note: Earpiece direction, diaphragm placement, and a quiet environment improve performance.

cards.back: A device that measures blood glucose from a small blood sample.
cards.note: Use approved infection-control technique, verify strip compatibility, and interpret the result with the patient presentation.

cards.back: Automated external defibrillator: analyzes rhythm and advises or delivers a shock when appropriate.
cards.note: Minimize interruptions in CPR and ensure no one is touching the patient during analysis or shock.

cards.back: An advanced device used for ECG monitoring, defibrillation, pacing, cardioversion, and other functions depending on configuration.
cards.note: EMTs should recognize the equipment even when operation is outside their scope.

cards.back: A device that may limit some neck movement as part of spinal-motion restriction.
cards.note: A collar does not fully immobilize the spine and should not distract from airway or other priorities.

cards.back: A full-body device that molds around the patient when air is removed.
cards.note: It can support comfortable motion restriction and transport in selected situations.

cards.back: A stretcher that separates into sections so it can be assembled around a patient.
cards.note: It can reduce rolling during lifting or transfer; secure the patient before movement.

cards.back: A rigid device useful for extrication and short transfers.
cards.note: Many systems avoid routine prolonged transport on a board because of discomfort and pressure concerns; follow local policy.

cards.back: A compact chair used to move seated patients on stairs or through tight spaces.
cards.note: Use the manufacturer’s straps, enough personnel, and clear commands.

cards.back: A device that applies longitudinal traction to selected isolated mid-shaft femur fractures.
cards.note: Indications and contraindications must be assessed before use.

cards.back: A device placed around the pelvis to reduce movement and support suspected unstable pelvic injury.
cards.note: Correct placement is generally over the greater trochanters, not the waist.

cards.back: A device used to control life-threatening extremity bleeding by compressing blood flow.
cards.note: Apply according to training, tighten until bleeding stops, record the time, and do not conceal it.

cards.back: Gauze treated or designed to support clot formation when packed into a bleeding wound.
cards.note: Use with firm direct pressure and according to product and protocol guidance.

cards.back: An airtight or water-resistant dressing used for selected open wounds, including some chest injuries.
cards.note: Monitor the patient closely because chest findings can change.

cards.back: A flexible splint, often foam-covered aluminum, that can be shaped to support an injured extremity.
cards.note: Assess circulation, sensation, and movement before and after splinting.

cards.back: Straps that secure a patient to the ambulance stretcher.
cards.note: Use all required restraints and shoulder straps; ambulance movement can create major forces.

cards.back: A drug class that includes prescription pain medicines and illicit substances such as heroin; effects can include pain relief, sedation, and respiratory depression.
cards.note: Look for slow or absent breathing and decreased responsiveness. Drug identity cannot be confirmed by appearance alone.

cards.back: A potent synthetic opioid used medically and also found in the illicit drug supply.
cards.note: Illicit fentanyl may be mixed into powders or counterfeit pills; treat the patient’s condition and use PPE and local protocol.

cards.back: An illicit opioid that can cause euphoria, sedation, pinpoint pupils, and life-threatening respiratory depression.
cards.note: Route and appearance vary; do not delay ventilation and overdose care while trying to identify the substance.

cards.back: Illicitly manufactured tablets made to resemble prescription medications.
cards.note: They may contain unexpected fentanyl or other substances, so markings and color do not prove contents.

cards.back: A stimulant that can increase heart rate, blood pressure, temperature, agitation, and risk of chest pain or dysrhythmia.
cards.note: Crack is a smokable form of cocaine; both can produce serious cardiovascular emergencies.

cards.back: A powerful stimulant that can cause agitation, paranoia, hyperthermia, tachycardia, and hypertension.
cards.note: Consider scene safety, temperature, glucose, trauma, and co-ingestants.

cards.back: A synthetic drug with stimulant and perception-altering effects.
cards.note: Possible concerns include hyperthermia, dehydration or overhydration, agitation, and serotonin-related toxicity.

cards.back: A drug containing cannabinoids such as THC that can alter perception, coordination, heart rate, and anxiety.
cards.note: Effects vary by dose, route, product, age, and co-ingestants.

cards.back: Laboratory-made chemicals intended to act on cannabinoid receptors, often with unpredictable effects.
cards.note: Agitation, seizures, vomiting, altered mental status, and cardiovascular effects can occur.

cards.back: Phencyclidine, a dissociative drug that can cause severe agitation, altered perception, numbness, hypertension, and unpredictable behavior.
cards.note: Prioritize safety and avoid relying on pain response as the only assessment.

cards.back: Ketamine is a dissociative anesthetic used medically and sometimes misused recreationally.
cards.note: Effects may include dissociation, impaired movement, vomiting, and altered consciousness; medical ketamine use is distinct from illicit use.

cards.back: A hallucinogen that can cause altered perception, anxiety, panic, and impaired judgment.
cards.note: Serious illness may be related to behavior, trauma, co-ingestants, or an unexpected substance.

cards.back: Hallucinogenic mushrooms that can alter perception, mood, and thinking.
cards.note: Supportive care, safety, and assessment for co-ingestants or trauma may be important.

cards.back: A central nervous system depressant that can produce rapid sedation, vomiting, and respiratory compromise.
cards.note: Patients may alternate between deep sedation and agitation; protect the airway and reassess frequently.

cards.back: Synthetic stimulants that may mimic effects of cocaine, methamphetamine, or MDMA.
cards.note: Possible findings include severe agitation, paranoia, hyperthermia, tachycardia, and hypertension.

cards.back: A veterinary sedative increasingly found mixed with illicit drugs, especially opioids.
cards.note: Naloxone can treat an accompanying opioid component but does not reverse xylazine itself; ventilation and supportive care remain essential.

cards.back: Misuse of sedative medications such as alprazolam or diazepam can cause drowsiness, poor coordination, and respiratory depression, especially with opioids or alcohol.
cards.note: Counterfeit tablets may contain unexpected substances.

cards.back: Fumes from household or industrial products inhaled for intoxicating effects.
cards.note: They can cause hypoxia, dysrhythmias, neurologic changes, burns, or chemical exposure.

cards.back: Use of more than one drug or substance, intentionally or unknowingly.
cards.note: Mixed stimulants, depressants, alcohol, or counterfeit products can create atypical presentations.

cards.back: A recognizable pattern of findings associated with a class of toxins.
cards.note: Toxidromes guide assessment but do not prove the exact substance; always consider medical mimics.

cards.back: A medical gas used to treat or prevent hypoxemia in selected patients.
cards.note: Target, device, and flow should follow patient need and local protocol; oxygen is a medication.

cards.back: An antiplatelet medication commonly used in suspected acute coronary syndrome when indicated.
cards.note: Check allergies, bleeding concerns, and protocol; do not teach yourself a dose from a flashcard.

cards.back: A concentrated glucose preparation used for selected patients with suspected or confirmed hypoglycemia who can protect their airway and swallow.
cards.note: Airway status and ability to follow commands matter.

cards.back: An opioid antagonist that can reverse opioid-related respiratory depression.
cards.note: Ventilation remains a priority; patients can become acutely ill or agitated as opioid effects reverse.

cards.back: A device that delivers epinephrine for severe allergic reactions or anaphylaxis.
cards.note: EMT administration or assistance depends on state scope and local protocol.

cards.back: A bronchodilator used for bronchospasm in conditions such as asthma or COPD.
cards.note: It may increase heart rate or cause tremor; assessment and local protocol guide use.

cards.back: A vasodilator commonly prescribed for angina and used in some EMS chest-pain or pulmonary-edema protocols.
cards.note: Blood pressure, contraindications, prescribed medication status, and medical-control rules matter.

cards.back: A pain reliever and fever reducer.
cards.note: Some EMS systems allow EMT use; consider allergies, duplicate products, liver disease, and protocol.

cards.back: A nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug used for pain and fever.
cards.note: Some EMS systems allow EMT use; consider bleeding, kidney disease, pregnancy, allergies, and protocol.

cards.back: An adsorbent historically used for selected oral poisonings.
cards.note: Use has become limited in many systems; aspiration risk and poison-control or medical-direction guidance are important.

cards.back: A hormone medication that raises blood glucose and may be used when glucose cannot be given by mouth or IV.
cards.note: Scope and route vary; nausea and vomiting can occur.

cards.back: An intravenous or intraosseous glucose solution used to treat hypoglycemia.
cards.note: This is usually an ALS medication; concentration and extravasation risks require training.

cards.back: An antiemetic used to reduce nausea and vomiting.
cards.note: Route, contraindications, and cardiac considerations depend on protocol.

cards.back: A potent opioid analgesic used in controlled medical settings for pain management.
cards.note: Medical fentanyl and illicit fentanyl involve different contexts; respiratory and hemodynamic monitoring are essential.

cards.back: An opioid analgesic used in some EMS systems for pain and selected cardiovascular conditions.
cards.note: It can cause respiratory depression and hypotension; indications have evolved across protocols.

cards.back: A dissociative medication used by appropriately credentialed clinicians for analgesia, sedation, or severe agitation in some systems.
cards.note: Use requires protocol, monitoring, airway readiness, and careful documentation.

cards.back: An anticholinergic medication used for selected symptomatic bradycardia and certain poisonings.
cards.note: Indications and dosing are ALS-level protocol topics.

cards.back: A short-acting antiarrhythmic used for selected regular narrow-complex tachycardias.
cards.note: Correct rhythm identification, rapid administration technique, and monitoring are essential.

cards.back: An antiarrhythmic medication used in selected ventricular dysrhythmias.
cards.note: Indication and administration differ between cardiac arrest and perfusing rhythms.

cards.back: A medication used in selected conditions such as torsades de pointes, severe asthma, or eclampsia depending on protocol.
cards.note: It is generally an ALS medication requiring monitoring.

cards.back: A safety framework that includes the right patient, medication, dose, route, time, and documentation, with additional rights used by some systems.
cards.note: A mnemonic supports—but does not replace—indication, contraindication, allergy, interaction, and reassessment checks.

cards.back: The medications an EMT may administer, assist with, or monitor differ by state and agency.
cards.note: Your course, medical director, and current protocol are the source of authority.

cards.back: The initial process of evaluating safety, mechanism or nature of illness, number of patients, needed resources, and spinal-motion concerns.
cards.note: It begins before patient contact and continues as conditions change.

cards.back: A rapid overall judgment of how ill or injured the patient appears.
cards.note: Age, position, work of breathing, skin, behavior, and environment contribute.

cards.back: A rapid evaluation focused on immediate life threats involving airway, breathing, circulation, disability, and exposure as taught by the course.
cards.note: The exact sequence may vary, but life threats are addressed promptly.

cards.back: The main symptom, problem, or reason the patient says EMS was called.
cards.note: The patient’s words can be more useful than a diagnostic label.

cards.back: The medical reason or symptom pattern leading to the call.
cards.note: Examples include breathing difficulty, chest discomfort, seizure, or altered mental status.

cards.back: How force or energy caused a traumatic injury.
cards.note: Mechanism helps predict injuries but does not replace examination.

cards.back: A structured history: Signs/Symptoms, Allergies, Medications, Past history, Last oral intake, Events.
cards.note: Some courses or agencies use slight variations.

cards.back: A symptom-assessment framework: Onset, Provocation/Palliation, Quality, Region/Radiation, Severity, Time.
cards.note: Use natural conversation rather than sounding like a checklist.

cards.back: The first reliable set of measurements used for comparison during care.
cards.note: Document when and how they were obtained.

cards.back: Comparing repeated findings over time rather than relying on one measurement.
cards.note: A change in mental status, pulse, respirations, skin, or pressure can be more important than one isolated value.

cards.back: The patient’s degree of awareness and ability to respond.
cards.note: Assess changes and consider causes such as hypoxia, hypoglycemia, stroke, trauma, toxins, or seizure.

cards.back: A rapid responsiveness scale: Alert, responds to Verbal stimulus, responds to Pain, Unresponsive.
cards.note: AVPU is a snapshot and does not replace a fuller neurologic assessment.

cards.back: The number of palpable or monitored heartbeats per minute.
cards.note: Also assess regularity, strength, and location.

cards.back: The number of breaths per minute.
cards.note: Observe rate, depth, rhythm, effort, sounds, and chest movement before alerting the patient when possible.

cards.back: The force of circulating blood against arterial walls, commonly recorded as systolic over diastolic pressure.
cards.note: Interpret pressure with mental status, pulse, skin signs, history, and trends.

cards.back: An estimate of peripheral oxygen saturation measured by pulse oximetry.
cards.note: It does not directly measure ventilation and can be affected by artifact or poor perfusion.

cards.back: Color, temperature, moisture, and condition of the skin.
cards.note: These observations can reflect perfusion, temperature, stress response, or local injury.

cards.back: The time for color to return after blanching a nail bed or skin area.
cards.note: It is influenced by age, temperature, lighting, and perfusion and should not be used alone.

cards.back: Evaluation of pupil size, equality, shape, reactivity, and sometimes gaze.
cards.note: Findings should be interpreted with neurologic status, medications, lighting, and eye history.

cards.back: Glasgow Coma Scale: a structured score based on eye, verbal, and motor responses.
cards.note: Record the component scores, not just the total.

cards.back: A standardized check for findings such as facial asymmetry, arm weakness, speech changes, balance, or vision depending on the tool.
cards.note: Document last known well and follow local stroke-routing criteria.

cards.back: A focused or head-to-toe examination guided by the patient’s condition, history, and mechanism.
cards.note: It follows management of immediate threats.

cards.back: A trauma-assessment mnemonic: Deformities, Contusions, Abrasions, Punctures/Penetrations, Burns, Tenderness, Lacerations, Swelling.
cards.note: Use it as a prompt, not as a substitute for observation and palpation.

cards.back: Repeating the primary assessment, vital signs, interventions, and focused exam to identify change.
cards.note: Frequency depends on patient stability and local expectations.

cards.back: A concise transfer of essential patient information and care to the receiving clinician.
cards.note: Include identifiers, complaint, relevant history, findings, trends, interventions, response, and safety concerns.

cards.back: Infection-control practices used with every patient based on anticipated exposure.
cards.note: Select gloves, eye protection, mask, gown, and hand hygiene according to risk.

cards.back: Personal protective equipment used to reduce exposure to blood, body fluids, respiratory hazards, chemicals, or physical hazards.
cards.note: PPE must match the hazard and does not make an unsafe scene safe.

cards.back: The ongoing evaluation of threats to responders, patients, and bystanders.
cards.note: Violence, traffic, fire, electricity, animals, weather, and unstable structures are examples.

cards.back: Maintaining an accurate picture of the environment, patient, team, hazards, and changing priorities.
cards.note: Avoid tunnel vision and speak up when something changes.

cards.back: Using posture, positioning, and coordinated movement to reduce injury during lifting and moving.
cards.note: Keep loads close, communicate, use equipment, and request help early.

cards.back: Securing patients, providers, equipment, and loose objects during transport.
cards.note: Unrestrained occupants and equipment can become projectiles.

cards.back: Practices that reduce needle-stick and cutting injuries.
cards.note: Use approved containers, avoid unnecessary recapping, and report exposures promptly.

cards.back: Recognizing a possible hazardous-material incident and avoiding entry or contamination.
cards.note: Approach uphill, upwind, and upstream when appropriate and follow incident command.

cards.back: Sorting patients based on urgency and available resources.
cards.note: Systems and categories vary; use the method adopted by your agency.

cards.back: A standardized structure for managing roles, communication, and resources at incidents.
cards.note: Know who you report to and avoid freelancing.

cards.back: A concise transmission to dispatch, other units, or a receiving facility.
cards.note: Use plain language, protect privacy, and follow local format.

cards.back: The legal and clinical record of assessment, care, response, and disposition.
cards.note: Be objective, complete, timely, and consistent.

cards.back: Permission from a patient with decision-making capacity after appropriate explanation.
cards.note: Consent can be expressed verbally or through actions, depending on the situation.

cards.back: A legal concept allowing emergency care when a patient cannot consent and a reasonable person would want lifesaving treatment.
cards.note: Application depends on law, circumstances, and protocol.

cards.back: The ability to understand information, appreciate consequences, reason about options, and communicate a choice.
cards.note: Capacity is decision-specific and can change.

cards.back: The legal range of care a credentialed clinician is permitted to provide.
cards.note: It is defined by law, regulation, certification level, and system authorization.

cards.back: A medical-director-approved guideline that directs assessment and treatment within a system.
cards.note: Protocols do not replace judgment, but they define authorized care.

cards.back: Physician oversight of EMS care through standing orders, online consultation, quality improvement, and education.
cards.note: Know when your protocol requires contact.

cards.back: Using communication, leadership, role clarity, cross-checks, and shared situational awareness to improve safety.
cards.note: Closed-loop communication helps confirm that tasks were heard and completed.
